examples.text: Scientists measure modern plate motion using GNSS networks! They record a station's position over years and convert tiny shifts into velocity.
Tectonic plates move just a few centimeters per year — about as fast as your fingernail grows! Scientists measure this slow movement using GPS satellites.
Scientists measure modern plate motion using GNSS networks! They record a station's position over years and convert tiny shifts into velocity.
A single GPS reading is not a plate velocity! Scientists need a long time series so seasonal wiggles do not hide the slow displacement.

There are three plate boundaries: convergent — plates collide and one subducts or land crunches up; divergent — plates move apart and new crust forms; transform — plates slide horizontally past each other with no crust created or destroyed.
The force of separation at a divergent boundary creates a tension zone, where shallow earthquakes may happen.

What happens when plates crash into each other?

At a convergent boundary, plates push and collide! This creates tall mountains, deep trenches, and lots of earthquakes and volcanoes.

Shear stress happens when two plates rub against each other in opposite directions at transform fault boundaries.
You can find the Philippine Trench on the eastern side of our country, right inside the Pacific Ocean!

On a Philippine map, label the Sierra Madre mountains in eastern Luzon, Mayon volcano in southeastern Luzon, the Philippine Fault crossing several islands, and the Philippine Trench east of the archipelago. Compare PHIVOLCS fault and trench maps with a topographic map. Look for patterns; nearby mountains and faults do not all mark separate major plate boundaries.

What is an ocean trench?

It's like a super long, narrow valley carved right into the seafloor!

Real crustal blocks rotate and deform; coastlines change. Use measured Philippine Sea Plate velocities with their reference frame for a real estimate, and never treat the whole archipelago as one rigid plate or the sketch as a certain prediction.

Use a USGS reference to distinguish slab pull, where a dense sinking slab pulls attached plate, from ridge push, gravity-driven motion away from an elevated ridge. Plates move over the deformable, mostly solid asthenosphere. Mantle flow and plate motion interact; avoid a picture of plates floating on a liquid ocean or riding a simple conveyor belt. Record the source and the model’s limits.

What pushes and pulls tectonic plates besides convection?

Two forces! 'Slab pull' — a sinking plate's weight drags it down. 'Ridge push' — a raised ridge pushes the plate away!

What lies beneath the lithosphere?

The asthenosphere! It is a hotter, softer part of the mantle where the tectonic plates above slowly slide.

What happens when one tectonic plate slides under another?

Deep ocean trenches form below, and volcanoes form above!

An oceanic plate descends beneath an overriding plate at a subduction zone. Locked contact can build strain released in earthquakes. Water released from the descending slab lowers the melting temperature of parts of the mantle above it; magma can feed a volcanic arc. This is different from claiming the entire sinking plate simply melts.

What happens as the plate sinks at the Philippine Trench?

It produces earthquakes! These are the earthquakes that PHIVOLCS carefully monitors.

When two plates push together, Earth's crust crumples and rises up — forming giant mountains like the Himalayas!

Compare a collision diagram of India and Eurasia forming the Himalayas with oceanic Nazca Plate subduction beneath South America at the Andes. Both involve convergence and crustal shortening, but the Andes also have a volcanic arc associated with subduction. A mountain’s height alone does not reveal its tectonic mechanism.

Global warming is the slow rise in Earth's average temperature over the past decades.
Positive feedback loops amplify climate change! For example, when ice melts, exposed land or sea absorbs more sunlight, making the temperature rise further.
Because the Earth is warming, large sheets of ice and glaciers at the poles and on mountains are melting!
Sea level rises for two reasons: ice on land melts and adds water to the ocean, and seawater expands as it warms up.
Sea level rises for two reasons: ice on land melts and adds water to the ocean, and seawater expands as it warms up.

Warming melts glaciers and ice sheets on land, adding water to the ocean. Seawater also expands as it warms. Both raise sea level. Melting floating sea ice has little direct effect on sea level because it already displaces water, though its loss can amplify warming.
Global warming is the slow rise in Earth's average temperature over the past decades.

What exactly is climate change?

Climate change is a long-term shift in the world's usual weather patterns and temperatures. It means our global weather is changing over a long time!
Too many greenhouse gases trap more heat, and the whole Earth slowly warms up!
Burning coal and fuel releases greenhouse gases that warm the planet and raise the sea!
When fossil fuels are burned, they release carbon dioxide! This gas causes pollution and global warming.

What happens when we burn fossil fuels?

Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide that warms the Earth!

During El Niño, the Philippines gets hotter and drier with less rain, so PAGASA watches closely for drought.
El Nino happens when trade winds weaken and warm water piles up in the eastern Pacific, which PAGASA monitors!
La Niña is the cool phase of ENSO! It brings the Philippines more rain, stronger westward winds, and a higher risk of flooding.

For a coastal community, preparing for flooding and protecting evacuation routes are adaptation to climate impacts. Reducing fossil-fuel use is mitigation because it lowers greenhouse-gas emissions. Compare local evidence and involve community planning: individual actions help, but effective protection also needs shared infrastructure and policy.

With no air resistance and level ground, a thrown object travels the farthest (greatest range) when launched at an angle of 45 degrees!

With a teacher, investigate a soft ball’s flight in a clear area. Hold release speed and height constant while varying angle; measure maximum height and horizontal range over repeated trials. Then keep angle fixed to compare speeds. The familiar 45° maximum-range result assumes no air resistance and equal release and landing heights; it is not a universal rule for basketball.
As a projectile flies, gravity pulls it down! This makes its vertical motion slow down while rising, and speed up while falling.

In an elastic collision, objects bounce apart without losing motion energy, so the total kinetic energy stays exactly the same before and after!

In an inelastic collision, total kinetic energy is not conserved: some becomes deformation, thermal energy or sound. The objects may rebound; sticking together is the special case called perfectly inelastic. Total momentum is conserved if the system has negligible net external impulse. Energy does not disappear.

A car crashing into a wall is an inelastic collision because the car deforms and much kinetic energy becomes sound and heat.

What cool toy uses pendulums to show how energy moves?

Newton's cradle! It has hanging balls in a row — release one, and only the far end ball swings out!

Use teacher-supervised low-speed carts to model a collision. Record masses and velocities before and after; label equal and opposite contact forces on different carts. Compare a spring-bumper rebound with carts that stick. An ideal elastic collision conserves kinetic energy; an inelastic collision converts some into other forms. Check external forces before claiming total momentum is conserved.

Momentum is a cool measure of an object's motion! It is exactly equal to its mass multiplied by its velocity.
Momentum has a specific direction because it depends on velocity, which always points in the direction of motion!
A heavier moving object has more momentum at the same speed, making it harder to stop! That’s why a big truck is tougher to stop than a bicycle.

With a teacher, compare low-speed carts on a level track with a soft stopping pad. Measure each mass and incoming velocity. First compare different masses at similar velocities; then keep mass fixed and vary velocity. Record stopping time and repeat. Calculate p = mv. Compare the stopping conditions too: more momentum requires more stopping impulse, but stopping time and force depend on the pad and friction. Never test with people or road vehicles.

The change in an object's momentum depends on how strong the force is and how long that force acts!

For the same change in momentum, increasing the stopping time reduces the average net force: Faverage = change in momentum ÷ time. This helps explain cushioning in a landing. It does not guarantee a smaller force at every instant; the force can vary during contact.
In a crash, an airbag inflates fast to give your head and chest more time to stop, making the hitting force much smaller!

A seatbelt holds you in place when a car suddenly stops, keeping you safe from flying forward!

An airbag makes your body stop more slowly during a crash, so the push on you feels much softer and safer!

What is a crumple zone?

Engineering sources say a crumple zone is a designed crush space in the front or rear! It’s not random damage, it helps the cabin decelerate over a longer time.

What is an isolated system in physics?

It is a setup where no outside forces like friction or air resistance interfere, so only the objects colliding affect each other!

What is a power plant?

A power plant is a large facility that generates electricity and sends it to homes through wires!

Trace a typical grid route: power plant → step-up transformer → high-voltage transmission → substation → distribution lines and transformers → meter and protected household circuits. For the same transmitted power, higher voltage means lower current and less heating loss in wires. Transformers lower voltage for local use; the meter records energy in kWh. Protective equipment and trained workers manage hazards. Electricity remains dangerous at household voltage; students should observe diagrams, not open equipment.

What happens to electricity at a substation?

At a substation, the high voltage is lowered before electricity is sent to homes in the area!

Always keep your hands dry when touching a plug or switch! Wet hands let electricity flow much more easily.
When unplugging a device, always hold the plug, not the cord, so the wire stays safe and undamaged!
Overloading one extension cord with many appliances creates excess heat that can melt wires and start a house fire!
An electric motor changes electrical energy into motion, which is exactly what makes things like a fan spin!

How does a generator make electricity?

By moving a magnet near a wire, a process called electromagnetic induction!
A hand-crank generator uses your muscle power to rotate a magnet inside a coil of wire! It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy that can light an LED!
Many motors and generators use electromagnets instead of permanent magnets because they are much easier to control and strengthen!

How do generators and motors work in the energy chain?

A generator changes mechanical energy into electrical energy! A motor changes it back. They are opposite steps in the exact same cycle!
On a sunny day it is better to use daylight than to switch on lights, to save electricity!

In a group, list useful ways to reduce wasted electricity at school or home. Estimate one example: switching off an unused 10 W lamp for 2 hours saves 20 Wh, or 0.02 kWh. Compare practicality, safety and who can help. Less electricity use can lower costs and reduce demand for fossil-fuel generation. Agree on an action and review results later; keep lighting needed for safe work and ask adults to handle plugs or equipment.

How can you easily save electricity at home?

Simply turning off lights you are not using saves electricity!

A color or temperature change, a new odor, gas bubbles or a solid precipitate can be clues to a chemical reaction. Record teacher-provided observations and compare with the starting materials. No single clue is proof: boiling water also bubbles without making a new substance. Seek evidence of a change in chemical identity. Never taste or directly smell an unknown sample, and never mix household cleaners for this activity.

Compare teacher-provided observations: dilute hydrochloric acid turns blue litmus red; sodium hydroxide solution turns red litmus blue; approximately neutral sodium chloride saline changes neither. Use an indicator chart rather than taste or touch. These are supervised laboratory chemicals. Not every salt solution is neutral; its ions determine how it affects pH.

Compare teacher-approved samples with a reference chart. Blue litmus turns red in an acid; red litmus turns blue in a base. Bromothymol blue is yellow in acidic solution, green near neutral and blue in basic solution. Use separate labelled portions, equal sample volumes and the same number of indicator drops for each comparison. Include known controls and repeat. Neither indicator alone proves a solution is a salt; some salts form acidic or basic solutions.

In a combination or synthesis reaction, two or more substances join together to form a single new product, like hydrogen and oxygen forming water!
In a decomposition reaction, a single substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances, which is often caused by heat or electricity!
In a decomposition reaction, one compound breaks apart into simpler substances! For example, electricity can split water into hydrogen and oxygen.

What happens in a single replacement reaction?

A more reactive element takes the place of another in a compound, like iron displacing copper!

What happens in a double replacement reaction?

Two compounds exchange their parts, called ions, to form two new compounds, and it often produces a solid precipitate!
When wood or gas burns completely, it produces carbon dioxide and water vapor!

The human body works hard to keep its temperature around 37 degrees Celsius, even when it's cold outside.

What is homeostasis?

Homeostasis is how your body keeps things like temperature and water stable using feedback — like sweating when you're hot!
The body keeps blood sugar balanced by using insulin to lower it and glucagon to raise it.

What happens if your blood pressure suddenly drops?

Receptors in your blood vessels sense the change and signal your brain, which then tells your heart to beat faster to bring the pressure back up.
Homeostasis only works within a limited range — at too high or too low a temperature, the body can no longer balance itself, and life is put in danger.

In negative feedback, when something in your body drifts away from normal, your body responds by reversing the change and bringing it back to balance.

Is all feedback in the body negative?

No! Childbirth uses positive feedback. The stretching of the uterine walls causes contractions that further stretch the walls, continuing until the baby is born.
Positive feedback amplifies a change, pushing the body further away from its starting state until a specific event is completed.

What is biotechnology?

Biotechnology uses living things like bacteria, yeast, and plants to make useful stuff — like food, medicine, and even fuel!
Biotechnology is used in many fields—from farming and medicine to solving crimes—by using living things or their parts to make useful products.

What is bromelain?

It's a special enzyme in pineapple that can soften meat and helps break down protein.
For fermentation to work safely, the jar, hands, and tools must be clean — dirty microbes that sneak in can take over and spoil the food.
Yeast isn't the only fermenter — bacteria sour food too, like in yogurt and buro, while yeast makes alcohol and gas.

Not all mold is bad — some kinds are actually used to make certain types of cheese!
Yogurt, cheese, and bagoong are all made with help from tiny microbes, in a process called fermentation.

How is soy sauce made?

It is made by fermenting soybeans for a long time with mold and bacteria, giving it a dark color and savory flavor!
The sap from nipa palm flowers can turn into vinegar when it's left to sour.

How does tuba turn into coconut vinegar?

Bacteria ferment the coconut sap tuba, converting alcohol into acetic acid!

Is nata de coco made of coconut meat?

No! Nata de coco is not chopped coconut meat — bacteria build it from coconut water, so it's really more like clear jelly.

Where does nata de coco come from?

Bacteria actually make it! They ferment coconut water and build up a thick, edible mat of cellulose — that becomes the chewy nata de coco.

Golden Rice is a GMO rice with extra genes that let it make beta-carotene — which the body turns into vitamin A — to help children who don't get enough.

How does Bt corn fight off caterpillars?

Bt corn is a GMO with an added gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, making it produce a protein that kills caterpillars that eat it — so less pesticide is needed.

In a logistic model, population growth slows near carrying capacity as resources become limiting. Food, water and shelter affect how many organisms can be supported; access to mates also affects reproduction. Carrying capacity changes with conditions, and real populations may fluctuate or overshoot rather than settle at a perfectly fixed number.
